disease_info: Schizoaffective Disorder (Depressive Type) is characterized by an uninterrupted period of illness during which there is a major depressive episode concurrent with symptoms typical of schizophrenia, such as delusions, hallucinations, and negative symptoms. A key diagnostic feature is the presence of psychotic symptoms for at least two weeks in the absence of prominent mood symptoms, distinguishing it from mood disorders with psychotic features. Over time, individuals often experience fluctuating intensity of mood and psychotic phenomena, with associated functional decline in work, relationships, and self‑care. The depressive type lacks manic or hypomanic episodes and can be challenging to differentiate from major depressive disorder with psychosis or schizophrenia with secondary depression, requiring careful attention to the temporal relationship between mood and psychotic symptoms.

narrative.personality: Lawrence is a quietly intense, perfectionistic man who channels his anxiety into meticulous organization and solitary creative pursuits like art, hiking, and playing the ukulele.
narrative.stressor: The onset of Lawrence’s difficulties followed a major restructuring at the restaurant where he worked, when new management increased volume expectations, cut staff, and frequently criticized minor errors in his previously well‑run dish area. His long‑standing tendency toward anxious perfectionism became increasingly rigid as he took on extra shifts and stayed late to keep everything in order, sacrificing sleep, social contact, and his usual grounding activities like hiking and visiting galleries. Over several months, he became more withdrawn at home, preoccupied with work mistakes and abstract worries about being secretly evaluated, and he found it harder to follow complex kitchen routines and his usual reading and journaling, which deeply unsettled someone who had always prided himself on his careful thinking. After nearly two years of progressive decline—missed shifts, difficulty training new staff, and his wife noticing he would sit for long periods unable to organize simple tasks—she persuaded him to see a psychiatrist when he admitted he was coming to work early because he no longer trusted his own judgment to keep the kitchen safe.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I can’t seem to think straight or make simple decisions anymore, even about basic things at work and at home.”

narrative.personality: Tiffiny is a warm, creative woman who takes pride in her retail skills and channels her artistic curiosity into colorful displays, journaling, and community arts activities.
narrative.stressor: Tiffiny’s problems began after the sudden death of the grandmother who had helped raise her and was her main emotional support, an event that occurred just as she was saving and planning to open a small community art shop. In the months following the funeral, she threw herself into work and volunteering at community theater, but gradually she stopped attending yoga classes, let her sketchbooks sit untouched, and spent more nights alone replaying memories and feeling that her future plans no longer had meaning without her grandmother’s encouragement. Her concentration at the register declined, she began making uncharacteristic cash‑handling mistakes, and she pulled back from friends and art activities, all while privately wrestling with increasingly persistent thoughts about whether life was worth continuing and what it would be like if she were no longer here. After coworkers noticed her tearfulness, extended breaks, and a journal entry left open in the break room hinting she was thinking about not waking up, her manager and an aunt convinced her to seek urgent psychiatric help.
narrative.chief_complaint: “Lately I keep thinking everyone would be better off if I just didn’t wake up, and I can’t get these thoughts about dying out of my head.”

narrative.personality: Alaa is a steady, methodical man who takes pride in his craftsmanship and mentoring at work, and finds joy in structured hobbies like choir singing, gardening, and carefully catalogued woodworking projects.
narrative.stressor: Alaa’s difficulties emerged after he developed new cardiovascular problems that led to brief hospitalizations and medical restrictions at work, disrupting the physical routine and sense of reliability that had anchored him for decades. Used to being the dependable one at the press and in his church and family roles, he struggled with needing more rest, cutting back on coaching softball, and feeling less agile around heavy machinery, which quietly shook his identity as a strong, capable provider. Over the next year and a half he became slower and more hesitant both at home and on the job, spending long stretches sitting in his workshop without starting projects, moving between tasks with unusual indecision, and skipping choir rehearsals because he felt weighed down and unable to keep up. His wife and adult daughter finally urged him to see a psychiatrist after coworkers reported that he had become markedly slowed and disengaged on the line, sometimes standing motionless by the press or, at other times, pacing the floor before simple adjustments he once handled effortlessly.
narrative.chief_complaint: “I feel like I’m either moving in slow motion or can’t sit still, and it’s getting in the way of my work and everything I usually do.”
